title: CLO International Academic Month Issue 3 (Part 1) Interactive Garment Pattern Development and Virtual Simulation of Ancient Costume
description: The third episode of the CLO Academic Monthly video is here! chunks.title: CLO International Academic Month Issue 3 (Part 1) Interactive Garment Pattern Development and Virtual Simulation of Ancient Costume
chunks.content: ## Overview of Interactive Garment Pattern Development and Virtual Simulation This section introduces the use of Kolo 3D software and Likert Design Concept software in the development and virtual simulation of garment patterns, focusing on fingerprint sensors in clothing and traditional costume modeling. It outlines the integration of 3D human body modeling, clothing pattern design, and virtual garment simulation for both modern and ancient clothing. --- ## Introduction to Kolo 3D Software and Fingerprint Sensor Development Kolo 3D software is a key tool for clothing design, development, and scientific research, enabling the creation of 3D clothing models through pattern modeling and sewing simulation. It is user-friendly and applicable beyond clothing, including 3D movies and animation. ### Fingerprint Sensor in Clothing Design - Developing a fingerprint sensor for clothing production requires significant experience, making it difficult for students or new industry professionals. - The sensor’s design must integrate tightly with garment structures, which traditional education or industry practice does not easily teach. - Kolo 3D software combined with Likert Design Concept software offers a solution to this challenge. - The process is divided into eight steps: - Steps 1-4: Use Kolo 3D for human body and clothing modeling. - Steps 5-8: Use Likert for advanced leather, car seats, and furniture design, adaptable for clothing pattern refinement. - Kolo’s primary function remains clothing modeling. --- ## 3D Clothing Development Process Using Kolo and Likert ### Step 1: Human Body Modeling - Begin with 3D human body modeling to establish a base for clothing design. - Adjustments to the human body model allow for different sizes and ease settings. - Parametric size adjustment (e.g., chest circumference) is easier in Kolo compared to direct curve modeling. ### Step 2: Clothing Modeling on Human Body - Clothing models are built on the human body model with particular attention to the back curve for expansion. - Adjustments are necessary to ensure the desired design style, such as collars and sleeves. - Clothing modeling can be limited by ease and tightness settings without parametric controls. ### Step 3: Curve Adjustment - Modify 2D patterns and 3D clothing models to refine design details. - This includes resizing collars, sleeves, and other garment features to match design intent. ### Step 4: Opening the Clothing Surface - Unfold the clothing surface to create a smooth base for drawing accurate 3D clothing structure lines (e.g., front center line, back center line, side seams). - Surface opening must preserve original surface area, shape, and mesh structure without adding elasticity, as elasticity alters sewing results. - Smooth surfaces facilitate accurate structure line drawing and subsequent pattern development. --- ## Drawing Clothing Structure Lines and Pattern Generation - Structure lines are drawn interactively on the opened 3D clothing surface according to design requirements. - These lines form closed 3D curves which, when unfolded, generate the 2D clothing pattern. - Post-processing on paper includes smoothing curves for industrial production readiness.

chunks.content: - Surface opening must preserve original surface area, shape, and mesh structure without adding elasticity, as elasticity alters sewing results. - Smooth surfaces facilitate accurate structure line drawing and subsequent pattern development. --- ## Drawing Clothing Structure Lines and Pattern Generation - Structure lines are drawn interactively on the opened 3D clothing surface according to design requirements. - These lines form closed 3D curves which, when unfolded, generate the 2D clothing pattern. - Post-processing on paper includes smoothing curves for industrial production readiness. - The method avoids traditional measurements (e.g., front chest width, collar depth) by relying on intuitive interactive line drawing. - This interactive paper design allows for integrated and customized garment pattern creation. --- ## Use of Likert Software for Pattern Refinement - Export the clothing and human body models in OBJ, FBX, or triangular mesh formats from Kolo. - Import these into Likert’s Design Concept module for further design of clothing structure lines on a smooth surface. - Structure lines form enclosed surfaces with different colors indicating areas (e.g., yellow, green, blue). - The enclosed surfaces are expanded (flattened) into 2D patterns. - Expansion requires equal triangular mesh areas and border lengths to maintain sewing accuracy. - Maintaining this geometric consistency ensures that side seams and edges match perfectly when sewn. --- ## Application Examples: Women’s Clothing and Style Adjustment - Designers start with style pictures and existing paper patterns. - Outline extraction from style images leads to initial fashion model construction. - Subsequent adjustments refine the 3D fashion model to align with the desired design effect (e.g., skirt length, looseness, collar size). - Opening the surface is crucial for accurate seam line drawing, especially with complex features such as pleats. - Designers have freedom to place structure lines based on their vision and garment style. - This approach works best for relatively simple, single-layer daily wear. - Complex garments with many wrinkles (e.g., wedding dresses) require additional steps like wrinkle removal before unfolding. --- ## Limitations and Suitability of the Method - The method is less effective for garments with many wrinkles or highly complex designs. - Requires some experience in board design and garment structure to use effectively. - Best suited for integrated clothes with fewer complications. - No traditional calculation or measurement lines are required, emphasizing an interactive and intuitive design approach. --- ## Integration with Other Software and Technologies - While Kolo software is sufficient for 3D clothing modeling and pattern design without programming skills, interactive 3D models require additional software like Unity or Unreal Engine (UE4/UE5) for VR or interactive applications. - Kolo models can be exported in FBX format for integration with game engines or virtual museums. - Examples include development of ancient Chinese clothing museums and 3D simulations for education and cultural heritage preservation. --- ## Virtual Simulation and Historical Costume Reconstruction - Kolo software enables virtual needle simulation and pattern pasting for ancient costume reconstruction.

chunks.content: --- ## Integration with Other Software and Technologies - While Kolo software is sufficient for 3D clothing modeling and pattern design without programming skills, interactive 3D models require additional software like Unity or Unreal Engine (UE4/UE5) for VR or interactive applications. - Kolo models can be exported in FBX format for integration with game engines or virtual museums. - Examples include development of ancient Chinese clothing museums and 3D simulations for education and cultural heritage preservation. --- ## Virtual Simulation and Historical Costume Reconstruction - Kolo software enables virtual needle simulation and pattern pasting for ancient costume reconstruction. - Historical clothing from Han, Tang, Song, Ming, and Qing dynasties have been modeled using 3D interaction. - The process involves: - Drawing patterns based on ancient paintings and artifacts. - Copying and modeling patterns in Kolo. - Opening surfaces and drawing structure lines. - Producing 3D virtual garments that can be flipped and sewn virtually. - This method supports heritage science and cultural preservation efforts. - Virtual displays can be enhanced using other software like Cinema 4D (C4D), Maya, or Sandy Marks for improved visual effects. --- ## Case Studies and Projects - Maandui Hanfu replica: A national art foundation project (2018) using Kolo for simulation and pattern development. - Tang Bi painting style costume: First 3D interaction extraction and modeling. - Ming Dynasty Wanli scroll clothing: Developed as a 3D interactive garment. - European palace clothing models: Created for use with VR glasses and virtual engines. - Museum projects: Integration of Kolo models into Unity and UE4 for realistic 3D viewing and virtual exhibitions. --- ## Summary Kolo 3D software, combined with Likert Design Concept, provides a comprehensive platform for interactive garment pattern development and virtual simulation. This approach enables: - Parametric human body modeling for accurate sizing. - Interactive 3D clothing design with intuitive structure line drawing. - Surface opening techniques that preserve garment geometry. - Seamless transition from 3D models to 2D industrial patterns. - Application in both modern clothing and historical costume reconstruction. - Integration with advanced visualization tools for VR and interactive exhibitions. While requiring some technical experience, this workflow supports efficient, accurate, and culturally significant garment design and simulation without heavy reliance on programming or traditional pattern drafting calculations.

It outlines the integration of 3D human body modeling, clothing pattern design, and virtual garment simulation for both modern and ancient clothing. --- ## Introduction to Kolo 3D Software and Fingerprint Sensor Development Kolo 3D software is a key tool for clothing design, development, and scientific research, enabling the creation of 3D clothing models through pattern modeling and sewing simulation. It is user-friendly and applicable beyond clothing, including 3D movies and animation. ### Fingerprint Sensor in Clothing Design - Developing a fingerprint sensor for clothing production requires significant experience, making it difficult for students or new industry professionals. - The sensor’s design must integrate tightly with garment structures, which traditional education or industry practice does not easily teach. - Kolo 3D software combined with Likert Design Concept software offers a solution to this challenge. - The process is divided into eight steps: - Steps 1-4: Use Kolo 3D for human body and clothing modeling. - Steps 5-8: Use Likert for advanced leather, car seats, and furniture design, adaptable for clothing pattern refinement. - Kolo’s primary function remains clothing modeling. --- ## 3D Clothing Development Process Using Kolo and Likert ### Step 1: Human Body Modeling - Begin with 3D human body modeling to establish a base for clothing design. - Adjustments to the human body model allow for different sizes and ease settings. - Parametric size adjustment (e.g., chest circumference) is easier in Kolo compared to direct curve modeling. ### Step 2: Clothing Modeling on Human Body - Clothing models are built on the human body model with particular attention to the back curve for expansion. - Adjustments are necessary to ensure the desired design style, such as collars and sleeves. - Clothing modeling can be limited by ease and tightness settings without parametric controls. ### Step 3: Curve Adjustment - Modify 2D patterns and 3D clothing models to refine design details. - This includes resizing collars, sleeves, and other garment features to match design intent. ### Step 4: Opening the Clothing Surface - Unfold the clothing surface to create a smooth base for drawing accurate 3D clothing structure lines (e.g., front center line, back center line, side seams). - Surface opening must preserve original surface area, shape, and mesh structure without adding elasticity, as elasticity alters sewing results. - Smooth surfaces facilitate accurate structure line drawing and subsequent pattern development. --- ## Drawing Clothing Structure Lines and Pattern Generation - Structure lines are drawn interactively on the opened 3D clothing surface according to design requirements. - These lines form closed 3D curves which, when unfolded, generate the 2D clothing pattern. - Post-processing on paper includes smoothing curves for industrial production readiness. - The method avoids traditional measurements (e.g., front chest width, collar depth) by relying on intuitive interactive line drawing. - This interactive paper design allows for integrated and customized garment pattern creation. --- ## Use of Likert Software for Pattern Refinement - Export the clothing and human body models in OBJ, FBX, or triangular mesh formats from Kolo. - Import these into Likert’s Design Concept module for further design of clothing structure lines on a smooth surface. - Structure lines form enclosed surfaces with different colors indicating areas (e.g., yellow, green, blue). - The enclosed surfaces are expanded (flattened) into 2D patterns. - Expansion requires equal triangular mesh areas and border lengths to maintain sewing accuracy. - Maintaining this geometric consistency ensures that side seams and edges match perfectly when sewn. --- ## Application Examples: Women’s Clothing and Style Adjustment - Designers start with style pictures and existing paper patterns. - Outline extraction from style images leads to initial fashion model construction. - Subsequent adjustments refine the 3D fashion model to align with the desired design effect (e.g., skirt length, looseness, collar size). - Opening the surface is crucial for accurate seam line drawing, especially with complex features such as pleats. - Designers have freedom to place structure lines based on their vision and garment style. - This approach works best for relatively simple, single-layer daily wear. - Complex garments with many wrinkles (e.g., wedding dresses) require additional steps like wrinkle removal before unfolding. --- ## Limitations and Suitability of the Method - The method is less effective for garments with many wrinkles or highly complex designs. - Requires some experience in board design and garment structure to use effectively. - Best suited for integrated clothes with fewer complications. - No traditional calculation or measurement lines are required, emphasizing an interactive and intuitive design approach. --- ## Integration with Other Software and Technologies - While Kolo software is sufficient for 3D clothing modeling and pattern design without programming skills, interactive 3D models require additional software like Unity or Unreal Engine (UE4/UE5) for VR or interactive applications. - Kolo models can be exported in FBX format for integration with game engines or virtual museums. - Examples include development of ancient Chinese clothing museums and 3D simulations for education and cultural heritage preservation. --- ## Virtual Simulation and Historical Costume Reconstruction - Kolo software enables virtual needle simulation and pattern pasting for ancient costume reconstruction. - Historical clothing from Han, Tang, Song, Ming, and Qing dynasties have been modeled using 3D interaction. - The process involves: - Drawing patterns based on ancient paintings and artifacts. - Copying and modeling patterns in Kolo. - Opening surfaces and drawing structure lines. - Producing 3D virtual garments that can be flipped and sewn virtually. - This method supports heritage science and cultural preservation efforts. - Virtual displays can be enhanced using other software like Cinema 4D (C4D), Maya, or Sandy Marks for improved visual effects. --- ## Case Studies and Projects - Maandui Hanfu replica: A national art foundation project (2018) using Kolo for simulation and pattern development. - Tang Bi painting style costume: First 3D interaction extraction and modeling. - Ming Dynasty Wanli scroll clothing: Developed as a 3D interactive garment. - European palace clothing models: Created for use with VR glasses and virtual engines. - Museum projects: Integration of Kolo models into Unity and UE4 for realistic 3D viewing and virtual exhibitions. --- ## Summary Kolo 3D software, combined with Likert Design Concept, provides a comprehensive platform for interactive garment pattern development and virtual simulation. This approach enables: - Parametric human body modeling for accurate sizing. - Interactive 3D clothing design with intuitive structure line drawing. - Surface opening techniques that preserve garment geometry. - Seamless transition from 3D models to 2D industrial patterns. - Application in both modern clothing and historical costume reconstruction. - Integration with advanced visualization tools for VR and interactive exhibitions. While requiring some technical experience, this workflow supports efficient, accurate, and culturally significant garment design and simulation without heavy reliance on programming or traditional pattern drafting calculations.
